newsitem.title: UK: Elf strike gives comfort to already firm fuel oil.
newsitem.headline: Elf strike gives comfort to already firm fuel oil.

text.p: A week-long strike by Elf Aquitaine refinery workers in France has helped nudge fuel oil prices higher in an already firm European market supported by recent buy tenders and tightish supplies.
"It's looking nice and strong," said one trader of the low sulphur market.
Now in its seventh day, the dispute has closed fuel oil output from the group's three refineries.
Elf is estimated to have combined fuel oil output of around 10,000 tonnes per day, so up to 70,000 tonnes of fuel has been lost so far.
The disruption of Elf's fuel oil output is coming at a time when the European market is firming in anticipation of increased winter demand.

On Wednesday French unions called a 24-hour strike at Royal Dutch/Shell Group's 129,000 barrels per day Berre refinery in southern France for Monday, December 9 over the company's plans to cut costs. The dispute may spread to Shell's other main French plant, the 140,000 bpd refinery at Petit Couronne.

Stocks of fuel oil are already also low compared with year ago levels, according to Euroilstock figures. Fuel oil stocks in Europe stood at 142 million barrels in October, down 6.55 percent from last year.

The low sulphur fuel market is becoming tight with two Turkish tenders for up to 90,000 tonnes for delivery in December balanced by only one 50,000 tonne cargo actively offered for the second half of the month.
A couple of smaller parcels are held by traders, but strong natural gas prices in the U.S. were likely to keep American fuel at home and may even draw some European product transatlantic.
At least one 50,000 tonne low sulphur cargo has already been sold to an American buyer and is expected to move west.

Elf has a contract with the world's biggest buyer of low sulphur fuel, Italian state utility Enel, and there has been market speculation about whether material might be lost as a result of the dispute.
"They (Elf) seem to have been scrabbling around recently," said one dealer.
Low sulphur has risen to around $135 fob NWE, against $132 before the strike.
The high sulphur sector looks more balanced than the low sulphur market, but tenders from Portugal and Turkey for up to 125,000 tonnes in December and January should act as props.
